claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma carries a dismal prognosis, with high rates of metastasis and few treatment options.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma carries a dismal prognosis, with high rates of metastasis and few treatment options.
evidence: This is a general statement about PDAC that draws from established scientific consensus about the disease characteristics.

claim: Hyperactivation of KRAS in almost all tumours drives RAC1 activation, conferring enhanced migratory and proliferative capacity as well as macropinocytosis.
source: Hyperactivation of KRAS in almost all tumours drives RAC1 activation, conferring enhanced migratory and proliferative capacity as well as macropinocytosis.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field about KRAS-RAC1 signaling pathways.

claim: CYRI-B is highly expressed in pancreatic tumours in a mouse model of KRAS and p53-driven pancreatic cancer.
source: We find that CYRI-B is highly expressed in pancreatic tumours in a mouse model of KRAS and p53-driven pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of Cyrib accelerates tumourigenesis, leading to enhanced ERK and JNK-induced proliferation in precancerous lesions.
source: Deletion of Cyrib (the gene encoding CYRI-B protein) accelerates tumourigenesis, leading to enhanced ERK and JNK-induced proliferation in precancerous lesions, indicating a potential role as a buffer of RAC1 hyperactivation in early stages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the CKPC mouse model showing increased pERK, pJNK, and BrdU staining in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of CYRI-B inhibits metastasis as disease progresses.
source: However, as disease progresses, loss of CYRI-B inhibits metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced metastasis in CKPC mice compared to KPC mice in Figure 4.

claim: CYRI-B depleted tumour cells show reduced chemotactic responses to lysophosphatidic acid.
source: CYRI-B depleted tumour cells show reduced chemotactic responses to lysophosphatidic acid, a major driver of tumour spread, due to impaired macropinocytic uptake of the lysophosphatidic acid receptor 1.
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Reduced chemotactic response in CYRI-B depleted cells is due to impaired macropinocytic uptake of LPAR1.
source: CYRI-B depleted tumour cells show reduced chemotactic responses to lysophosphatidic acid, a major driver of tumour spread, due to impaired macropinocytic uptake of the lysophosphatidic acid receptor 1.
evidence: This is supported by data showing CYRI-B co-localization with LPAR1 in macropinosomes (Figure 8) and impaired LPAR1 internalization in CYRI-B depleted cells (Figure 9).

claim: PDAC is thought to arise from precancerous non-invasive pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasms (PanINs) classified as PanIN1–3.
source: PDAC is thought to arise from precancerous non-invasive pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasms (PanINs) classified as PanIN1–3 depending on the molecular and histological characteristics (Hruban et al., 2001; Hruban et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PanINs arise from acinar cells that undergo acinar to ductal metaplasia changes.
source: PanINs arise from acinar cells that undergo acinar to ductal metaplasia changes (Wang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The KPC mouse model recapitulates multiple features of human PDAC disease.
source: the current gold standard mouse model of metastatic PDAC - the KPC (KRASG12D, p53R172H, Pdx-1-Cre) (Hingorani et al., 2005) recapitulates multiple features of the human disease (Hwang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing the KPC model.

claim: Cytoskeletal and migration-associated proteins have been associated with aggression and metastasis in PDAC in human patient transcriptomes.
source: Cytoskeletal and migration-associated proteins have been associated with aggression and metastasis in PDAC both in human patient transcriptomes (Bailey et al., 2016) and in the KPC mouse model (Juin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Deletion of RAC1 in a KRAS-driven mouse model of PDAC delayed tumour onset, reduced PanIN lesions, and improved survival.
source: Deletion of RAC1 in a KRAS-driven mouse model of PDAC delayed tumour onset, reduced PanIN lesions, and improved survival (Heid et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dysregulation of RAC1 control of epithelial polarity by active KRAS drives acinar to ductal metaplasia and accelerates tumourigenesis.
source: This led to the conclusion that dysregulation of RAC1 control of epithelial polarity by active KRAS drives acinar to ductal metaplasia and accelerates tumourigenesis (Heid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RAC1 regulates polarity and migration via Scar/WAVE-Arp2/3 control of actin dynamics at cell-cell contacts and at the cell leading edge.
source: RAC1 regulates polarity and migration via Scar/WAVE-Arp2/3 control of actin dynamics at cell-cell contacts and at the cell leading edge.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about RAC1 signaling pathways.

claim: Coordinated RAC1 activation and deactivation are important in macropinocytosis.
source: Additionally, coordinated RAC1 activation and deactivation are important in macropinocytosis, an actin-driven process whereby cells engulf extracellular substances via large cup-shaped protrusions of the plasma membrane (Egami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Extracellular stimulation of cell surface receptors can trigger macropinocytosis via RAC1 and the Scar/WAVE complex.
source: Extracellular stimulation of cell surface receptors, such as tyrosine kinase or G-protein-coupled receptors, can trigger macropinocytosis via RAC1 and the Scar/WAVE complex (Buckley and King, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Macropinocytosis is a major way for PDAC tumours to take up proteins, lipids, and cell debris from their environment.
source: Tumours are frequently starved for amino acids and other nutrients and macropinocytosis is a major way for PDAC tumours to take up proteins, lipids, and cell debris from their environment (Commisso et al., 2013; Hobbs and Der, 2022; Kamphorst et al., 2015; Puccini et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Macropinocytosis provides cells with a mechanism for internalisation of signalling receptors.
source: Macropinocytosis also provides cells with a mechanism for internalisation of signalling receptors (Clayton and Cousin, 2009; Le et al., 2021; Stow et al., 2020), but whether this has consequences for tumour progression is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pancreatic cancer cells migrate towards lysophosphatidic acid both in vitro and in vivo, contributing to metastasis.
source: Chemotaxis is thought to be a key driver of metastasis and pancreatic cancer cells migrate towards lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) both in vitro and in vivo, contributing to metastasis (Juin et al., 2019; Papalazarou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: LPA was previously found to be consumed by melanoma and PDAC cells creating self-generated gradients contributing to metastasis.
source: LPA is a serum-derived chemotactic factor and was previously found to be consumed by melanoma and PDAC cells creating self-generated gradients contributing to metastasis (Juin et al., 2019; Muinonen-Martin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B protein was discovered to interact with RAC1 and enhance leading edge actin dynamics by negatively regulating activation of the Scar/WAVE complex.
source: Recently, the CYRI-B protein (Cyfip-related RAC1-interacting protein B, formerly known as Fam49-B) was discovered to interact with RAC1 and enhance leading edge actin dynamics by negatively regulating activation of the Scar/WAVE complex (Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Scar/WAVE is a pentameric complex that interacts with both RAC1 and Arp2/3 complex and triggers actin assembly in lamellipodia.
source: Scar/WAVE is a pentameric complex that interacts with both RAC1 and Arp2/3 complex and triggers actin assembly in lamellipodia (Insall and Machesky, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Depletion of CYRI-B in cultured cells enhanced lamellipodia stability, but did not impair migration speed.
source: Depletion of CYRI-B in cultured cells enhanced lamellipodia stability, but did not impair migration speed (Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI proteins play an important role in macropinocytosis, via the RAC1-Scar/WAVE pathway.
source: CYRI proteins also play an important role in macropinocytosis, via the RAC1-Scar/WAVE pathway (Le et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Cyrib gene resides on human chromosome 8q24, near c-Myc, and is frequently amplified in many types of cancer, including pancreatic cancer.
source: The Cyrib gene resides on human chromosome 8q24, near c-Myc, and is frequently amplified in many types of cancer, including pancreatic cancer (Nikolaou and Machesky, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: High expression of CYRI-B correlates with poor outcome in many cancers, including in human pancreatic cancer.
source: High expression of CYRI-B correlates with poor outcome in many cancers (Li et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022a), including in human pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In the KPC model, PanIN develops by around 10 weeks and progresses to later stages towards 15 weeks, with full-blown PDAC appearing at this stage.
source: In this model, PanIN develops by around 10 weeks and progresses to later stages towards 15 weeks, with full-blown PDAC appearing at this stage and mice reaching end-point with a half time of median 150–200 days.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the KPC model progression.

claim: At 6 weeks, before appearance of PanIN, Cyrib was not detected in the pancreas.
source: At 6 weeks, before appearance of PanIN, Cyrib was not detected in the pancreas (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cyrib expression was detectable by 10 weeks, especially around PanIN lesions, which remained stable until 15 weeks of age.
source: Cyrib expression was detectable by 10 weeks, especially around PanIN lesions, which remained stable until 15 weeks of age (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: End-point tumours showed a significant increase in the levels of Cyrib.
source: End-point tumours showed a significant increase in the levels of Cyrib (Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ISH of end-point tumours confirmed no detectable Cyrib mRNA in CKPC tumours in comparison with KPC.
source: ISH of end-point tumours confirmed no detectable Cyrib mRNA in CKPC tumours in comparison with KPC (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Western blotting confirmed absence of CYRI-B protein in cell lines derived from end-point CKPC mouse tumours compared with a cell line from a KPC mouse tumour.
source: Western blotting also confirmed absence of CYRI-B protein in cell lines derived from end-point CKPC mouse tumours (CKPC-1 and CKPC-2) compared with a cell line from a KPC mouse tumour (KPC-1) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: KPC and CKPC end-point tumours showed no difference in the proliferation (Ki-67) or death (cleaved caspase-3, CC-3) of tumour cells.
source: KPC and CKPC end-point tumours showed no difference in the proliferation (Ki-67) or death (cleaved caspase-3, CC-3) of tumour cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: CKPC tumours did not show any significant change in the CD31 vessel density.
source: CKPC tumours also did not show any significant change in the CD31 vessel density (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: CKPC tumours did not show any significant change in necrosis.
source: CKPC tumours also did not show any significant change in the CD31 vessel density (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F) or necrosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by histology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the median survival to end-point of CKPC mice (118 days) in comparison with the KPC mice (187 days).
source: However, there was a significant decrease in the median survival to end-point of CKPC mice (118 days) in comparison with the KPC mice (187 days) (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Loss of Cyrib did not affect the tumour weight to body mass ratio at end-point.
source: However, there was a significant decrease in the median survival to end-point of CKPC mice (118 days) in comparison with the KPC mice (187 days) (Figure 2E) without affecting the tumour weight to body mass ratio at end-point (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Loss of Cyrib in the pancreas accelerates progression to end-point of KRASG12D, p53R172H-driven PDAC in the KPC model.
source: Thus, loss of Cyrib in the pancreas accelerates progression to end-point of KRASG12D, p53R172H-driven PDAC in the KPC model, but does not grossly alter levels of cell growth/death or histological appearance of end-point tumours.
evidence: This is an inference based on the survival data and histological analysis presented.

claim: More PanIN2 and -3 lesions were present in 15-week-old CKPC mice over KPC controls.
source: Pancreatic samples from KPC or CKPC mice revealed no differences at 10 weeks, but more PanIN2 and -3 lesions were present in 15-week-old CKPC mice over KPC controls (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating an acceleration of early progression.
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the percentage pERK area from pancreata of CKPC mice vs KPC at 15 weeks.
source: Consistent with enhanced RAC1 signalling, we observed a significant increase in the percentage pERK area and pJNK area from pancreata of CKPC mice vs KPC (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: There was a significant increase in the percentage pJNK area from pancreata of CKPC mice vs KPC at 15 weeks.
source: Consistent with enhanced RAC1 signalling, we observed a significant increase in the percentage pERK area and pJNK area from pancreata of CKPC mice vs KPC (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Increased BrdU positive nuclei were found in the CKPC tissues in comparison with the KPC at 15 weeks.
source: We next investigated proliferation using BrdU injections at 15 weeks and found increased BrdU positive nuclei in the CKPC tissues in comparison with the KPC, suggesting enhanced proliferation in the abnormal ductal structures (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU staining data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: CKPC mice presented with increased pancreatic weight to body mass ratio at 15 weeks.
source: Indeed, CKPC mice presented with increased pancreatic weight to body mass ratio at 15 weeks, in agreement with increased proliferation of preneoplastic and neoplastic cells, whereas at 10 weeks of age there was no difference (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Loss of Cyrib in the KPC model accelerates PanIN formation and progression due to loss of CYRI-B's capacity to buffer RAC1 activation downstream of active KRAS.
source: Thus, loss of Cyrib in the KPC model accelerates PanIN formation and progression, likely due to loss of CYRI-B's capacity to buffer RAC1 activation downstream of active KRAS leading to abnormal architecture, combined with hyperactivation of ERK and JNK to drive proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased pERK, pJNK, and proliferation in CKPC mice.

claim: There was a significant reduction in metastasis to both the liver and bowel of CKPC mice compared to KPC mice.
source: Analysis of mice at end-point from KPC and CKPC cohorts revealed similar infrequent metastasis to the diaphragm in both cohorts, but a significant reduction in metastasis to both the liver and bowel of CKPC mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by metastasis incidence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the formation of small metastatic buds on mesentery in mice injected with Cyrib CRISPR KPC-1 cells.
source: Although the pancreas weight to body mass ratio did not change (Figure 4C), there was a significant reduction in the formation of small metastatic buds on mesentery in the mice injected with Cyrib CRISPR KPC-1 cells (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data from the in vivo transplantation assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No differences in proliferation were observed by Ki67 staining of tumours in the transplantation assay.
source: No differences in proliferation were observed by Ki67 staining of tumours (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There was a reduction in the number of mice with ascites fluid in mice bearing Cyrib CRISPR KPC-1 cells.
source: There was a reduction in the number of mice with ascites fluid in mice bearing Cyrib CRISPR KPC-1 cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CYRI-B is required for efficient metastatic seeding of KPC cells.
source: In summary, CYRI-B is required for efficient metastatic seeding of KPC cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced metastasis observed in CKPC mice and transplantation assays.

claim: CKPC-1 GFP cells presented with more lamellipodia, larger area, and increased ArpC2 recruitment to the leading edge in comparison with the rescued cells.
source: CKPC-1 GFP cells presented with more lamellipodia, larger area, and increased ArpC2 recruitment to the leading edge in comparison with the rescued cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E) in line with previous results for other cell types (Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: CKPC-1 cells (expressing GFP as a control) have dramatically reduced chemotactic potential towards FBS.
source: Both spider plots and rose plots showing the paths of individual cells and the mean resultant vector of migration, respectively, revealed that CKPC-1 cells (expressing GFP as a control) have dramatically reduced chemotactic potential towards FBS (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Re-expressing GFP-tagged CYRI-B in CKPC-1 cells fully restored chemotaxis and directed migration towards FBS.
source: On the contrary, re-expressing GFP-tagged CYRI-B in CKPC-1 cells fully restored chemotaxis and directed migration towards FBS (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Inhibition of LPAR1 and -3 by KI16425 abolished chemotactic steering in CKPC-1 rescued cells.
source: CKPC-1 rescued with GFP-tagged CYRI-B were also treated with LPA antagonist KI16425 (Ohta et al., 2003) showing that inhibition of LPAR1 and -3 by KI16425 abolished chemotactic steering, consistent with LPA being the major attractant in these conditions (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assay data with KI16425 treatment shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Deletion of Cyrib (Ex3 and Ex4) reduced chemotactic migration in comparison with control cells.
source: Deletion of Cyrib (Ex3 and Ex4) did not change the proliferation rate of cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but reduced chemotactic migration in comparison with control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: CYRI-B is required for chemotactic migration towards serum LPA in PDAC cells.
source: Therefore, CYRI-B is required for chemotactic migration towards serum LPA in PDAC cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemotaxis assay data showing reduced migration in CYRI-B depleted cells.

claim: CYRI-B was present on internal vesicles and tubules that connect with the vesicles.
source: Interestingly, CYRI-B was present on internal vesicles and tubules that connect with the vesicles (Figure 5A and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The lifetime of vesicular CYRI-B containing structures was around 40s.
source: The lifetime of vesicular CYRI-B containing structures was around 40s (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The average diameter of CYRI-B positive vesicles was about 1 μm.
source: The lifetime of vesicular CYRI-B containing structures was around 40s (Figure 5B), with an average diameter of about 1 μm (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The tubule length of CYRI-B positive structures ranged up to 17 μm.
source: whereas the tubule length ranged up to 17 μm (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CYRI-B localised at membrane cups.
source: Additionally, we noticed CYRI-B localising at membrane cups (Figure 5E and Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CYRI-B positive pseudopods extend nascent cups, fuse together, and they slowly move inside the cells with a mean lifetime of about 19s.
source: CYRI-B positive pseudopods extend nascent cups, fuse together, and they slowly move inside the cells with a mean lifetime of about 19s (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CYRI-B localised on structures resembling macropinocytic cups, vesicles, and associated tubules.
source: Thus, CYRI-B localised on structures resembling macropinocytic cups, vesicles, and associated tubules, similar to what we previously described for CYRI-A (Le et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data and comparison to prior work on CYRI-A.

claim: The CYRI-B positive cups and vesicles were in the size range of macropinosomes (0.2–5 μm).
source: The CYRI-B positive cups and vesicles were in the size range of macropinosomes (0.2–5 μm), rather than other endocytic vesicles and cups, which are typically less than 0.2 μm (Canton, 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison of measured sizes to established knowledge about macropinosome sizes.

claim: PDAC cells showed CYRI-B positive finger-like protrusions extending from the plasma membrane, until they fuse together engulfing extracellular dextran.
source: In agreement with this, PDAC cells showed CYRI-B positive finger-like protrusions extending from the plasma membrane, until they fuse together engulfing extracellular dextran (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CYRI-B positive pseudopods arising from the membrane enclose dextran, fuse together, and internalise in COS-7 cells.
source: Live-cell imaging of COS-7 cells transfected with CYRI-B-p17-GFP also showed that CYRI-B positive pseudopods arising from the membrane enclose dextran, fuse together, and internalise (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CYRI-B and Lck co-localised at the finger-like protrusions, cups, and internalised vesicles in AsPC-1 cells.
source: Live-cell imaging of AsPC-1 human pancreatic cancer cells transfected with CYRI-B-p17-GFP and mScarlet-Lck, a marker of the plasma membrane, showed that CYRI-B and Lck co-localised at the finger-like protrusions, cups, and internalised vesicles, confirming the localisation of CYRI-B on macropinosomes (Figure 7B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CYRI-B localises on macropinosomes in pancreatic cancer cell lines.
source: Thus, CYRI-B localises on macropinosomes in pancreatic cancer cell lines, suggesting a possible mechanism for how CYRI-B loss could affect tumour progression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data showing CYRI-B on macropinocytic structures.

claim: Rab5 is recruited after CYRI-B macropinosome internalisation, after ~50 s of internalisation.
source: After ~50 s of internalisation, Rab5 is recruited to the macropinosomes (Figure 7B and Figure 7—video 2), suggesting that CYRI-B is present prior to and also during early macropinosome formation as marked with Rab5.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CYRI-B is present prior to and also during early macropinosome formation as marked with Rab5.
source: After ~50 s of internalisation, Rab5 is recruited to the macropinosomes (Figure 7B and Figure 7—video 2), suggesting that CYRI-B is present prior to and also during early macropinosome formation as marked with Rab5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of CYRI-B and Rab5 recruitment observed in live-cell imaging.

claim: LPAR1-positive vesicles incorporated dextran and after some time they disappeared, with a mean lifetime of ~58 s.
source: We observed that LPAR1-positive vesicles incorporated dextran and after some time they disappeared, with a mean lifetime of ~58 s (Figure 8A, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LPAR1 is taken up from the cell surface by macropinocytosis.
source: Thus, LPAR1 is taken up from the cell surface by macropinocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of LPAR1 in dextran-positive vesicles.

claim: Upon CYRI-B internalisation, LPAR1 is also internalised with a lifetime of ~58 s in CKPC-1 cells.
source: Indeed, upon CYRI-B internalisation, LPAR1 is also internalised with a lifetime of ~58 s, consistent with LPAR-1 trafficking via CYRI-B positive macropinocytic events in PDAC cells (Figure 8B, Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: CKPC-1 cells expressing either GFP or CYRI-B-p17-GFP did not alter mRNA levels of LPAR1 or LPAR3.
source: Initial work showed that CKPC-1 cells expressing either GFP or CYRI-B-p17-GFP following stable transfection did not alter mRNA levels of LPAR1 or LPAR3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cyrib knockout cells (expressing GFP-only) showed high levels of leading edge membrane localisation of LPAR1 in comparison with the CYRI-B-p17-GFP rescued cells.
source: Cyrib knockout cells (expressing GFP-only) showed high levels of leading edge membrane localisation of LPAR1 in comparison with the CYRI-B-p17-GFP rescued cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: CYRI-B rescued cells showed a serum-stimulated enhancement of LPAR1 internalisation, while CYRI-B depleted cells showed minimal stimulation of LPAR1 uptake.
source: CYRI-B rescued cells showed a serum-stimulated enhancement of LPAR1 internalisation, while CYRI-B depleted cells showed minimal stimulation of LPAR1 uptake (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the image-based internalisation assay data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: The dependence of LPAR1 internalization on CYRI-B suggests that LPAR-1 is one cargo of CYRI-B-dependent macropinocytosis.
source: While LPAR1 may be internalised by multiple endocytic pathways, the dependence on CYRI-B suggests that LPAR-1 is one cargo of CYRI-B-dependent macropinocytosis, perhaps together with integrin and other receptors (e.g. Le et al., 2021), regulating surface levels and chemotactic migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing CYRI-B-dependent LPAR1 internalization and comparison to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B was highly expressed in human pancreatic cancers and correlated with poorer survival.
source: We noticed that CYRI-B was highly expressed in human pancreatic cancers and correlated with poorer survival (Nikolaou and Machesky, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Having a buffer for RAC1 activity could provide advantages for tumours, where mutations in KRAS will drive high activation of RAC1.
source: Having a buffer for RAC1 activity could provide advantages for tumours, where mutations in KRAS will drive high activation of RAC1, which might be detrimental to cell survival due to enhanced reactive oxygen species production and enhanced downstream signalling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of CYRI-B as a RAC1 buffer.

claim: CYRI-B could buffer RAC1 activity in early tumourigenesis.
source: These results support the idea that CYRI-B could buffer RAC1 activity in early tumourigenesis, but there are other possible explanations for its role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased pERK and pJNK in CKPC mice.

claim: Another study implicated CYRI-B in mitochondrial superoxide production, which could fuel early tumour progression.
source: Another study implicated CYRI-B in mitochondrial superoxide production, which could fuel early tumour progression (Chattaragada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Depletion of CYRI-B in MDCK cell spheroids disrupted lumen formation in a similar way to hyperactivation of RAC1.
source: We previously found that depletion of CYRI-B in MDCK cell spheroids disrupted lumen formation in a similar way to hyperactivation of RAC1.
evidence: This is a reference to prior unpublished or published work by the authors.

claim: RAC1 and PI3-kinase are important for apicobasal polarity in the pancreas.
source: Likewise, RAC1 and PI3-kinase are important for apicobasal polarity in the pancreas (Löf-Öhlin et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RAC1 has a known role in acinar to ductal metaplasia and in polarity and cell identity during early PDAC progression.
source: and RAC1 has a known role in acinar to ductal metaplasia and in polarity and cell identity during early PDAC progression (Heid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B has been implicated in PI3-kinase signalling in gallbladder cancer cells.
source: PI3-kinase plays an important role in polarity maintenance and CYRI-B has been implicated in PI3-kinase signalling in gallbladder cancer cells (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of CYRI-B could lead to hyperactivation or inappropriate spatial control of RAC1 activation causing a loss of normal cell polarity and therefore enhancing preneoplasia and cancer progression.
source: Loss of CYRI-B could therefore lead to hyperactivation or inappropriate spatial control of RAC1 activation causing a loss of normal cell polarity and therefore enhancing preneoplasia and cancer progression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism by which CYRI-B loss affects cancer progression.

claim: CYRI-B autoantibodies were detected as a potential biomarker for early stage breast cancer.
source: CYRI-B autoantibodies were detected as a potential biomarker for early stage breast cancer (Luo et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B was found in patient serum on extrachromosomal circular DNA overexpressed in lung adenocarcinoma.
source: a gene found in patient serum on extrachromosomal circular DNA overexpressed in lung adenocarcinoma (Xu et al., 2022b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B was highlighted as a potential saliva marker of oral cancer.
source: and a potential saliva marker of oral cancer (Kawahara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B was highlighted as a target of the zinc finger RNA-binding protein Zfrbp, leading to accelerated tumour development when overexpressed in colorectal and liver cancers.
source: CYRI-B was also highlighted as a target of the zinc finger RNA-binding protein Zfrbp, leading to accelerated tumour development when overexpressed in colorectal and liver cancers (Long et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Multiple studies suggest that CYRI-B may be enriched in extracellular vesicles associated with cancer and other diseases.
source: Multiple studies also suggest that CYRI-B may be enriched in extracellular vesicles associated with cancer and other diseases (e.g. Peng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B may have potential as a biomarker and driver of early cancer and play a role in the progression or conversion from precancerous to cancerous lesions.
source: Taken together, CYRI-B may have potential as a biomarker and driver of early cancer and play a role in the progression or conversion from precancerous to cancerous lesions, but more studies are needed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the collective evidence from multiple studies.

claim: N-WASP localises to SNX9-positive membrane tubules that are involved in trafficking of LPAR1 back to the plasma membrane after internalisation.
source: We previously found that loss of N-WASP in the KPC model caused a reduction in metastasis and that the role of N-WASP in recycling the LPA receptor LPAR1 was crucial in mediating this phenotype (Juin et al., 2019). While N-WASP localises to SNX9-positive membrane tubules that are involved in trafficking of LPAR1 back to the plasma membrane after internalisation, we find that CYRI-B is required for efficient internalisation of LPAR1 after stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CYRI-B and N-WASP control two different aspects of a similar pathway, whereby LPAR1 is stimulated, internalised, and then either sorted into tubules for rapid recycling or targeted towards lysosomes for slow recycling or degradation.
source: Thus, CYRI-B and N-WASP control two different aspects of a similar pathway, whereby LPAR1 is stimulated, internalised, and then either sorted into tubules for rapid recycling or targeted towards lysosomes for slow recycling or degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from this study and prior work on N-WASP.

claim: CYRI-B is important for protrusion dynamics and dynamics is essential for chemotaxis.
source: However, we previously showed that CYRI-B is important for protrusion dynamics and that dynamics, e.g., assembly and rapid disassembly, is essential for chemotaxis (Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells with too much RAC1 activity and delocalised RAC1 activity do not chemotax effectively.
source: Cells with too much RAC1 activity and delocalised RAC1 activity do not chemotax effectively. They rather require a balance of activation and inactivation (Pankov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: With macropinocytosis, RAC1 needs to be transiently activated to allow actin assembly and cup formation, but then RAC1 is dampened and actin needs to be disassembled to allow closure and uptake of macropinosomes or phagocytic vesicles into the cell.
source: Similarly, with macropinocytosis, RAC1 needs to be transiently activated to allow actin assembly and cup formation, but then RAC1 is dampened and actin needs to be disassembled to allow closure and uptake of macropinosomes or phagocytic vesicles into the cell (Le et al., 2021; Schlam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A major mechanism for internalisation of LPAR1 appears to be via macropinocytosis.
source: Interestingly, a major mechanism for internalisation of LPAR1 appears to be via macropinocytosis, as we observed LPAR1 on the membrane surface of both nascent and internalised macropinocytic structures co-localising with CYRI-B.
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data showing LPAR1 in CYRI-B-positive macropinosomes.

claim: There was a significant retardation of LPAR1 internalisation in CYRI-B depleted cells.
source: We also found a significant retardation of LPAR1 internalisation in CYRI-B depleted cells, indicating that LPAR1 is significantly internalised via CYRI-B-dependent macropinocytosis in PDAC cells.
evidence: This is supported by the internalisation assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Macropinocytosis is a key mechanism by which cells control surface receptor trafficking.
source: This suggests that macropinocytosis, which has recently attracted substantial interest as a regulator of nutrient uptake by PDAC cells (Canton, 2018; Commisso et al., 2013; Michalopoulou et al., 2020; Puccini et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2019), is also a key mechanism by which cells control surface receptor trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing LPAR1 trafficking via macropinocytosis and citations to prior work on macropinocytosis in nutrient uptake.

claim: Involvement of macropinocytosis in receptor trafficking has been previously observed, primarily in immune cells.
source: Although involvement of macropinocytosis in receptor trafficking has been previously observed (reviewed in Stow et al., 2020), studies are primarily in immune cells, which perform high levels of constitutive uptake.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.
